analysis.one_liner: Adds union recertification elections, supermajority strike votes, and strict limits on how unions spend dues.
analysis.headline: The Employee Rights Act, introduced by Senator Hatch with 31 Republican cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died in the Senate HELP Committee when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it harder for unions to organize workers and keep representing them. It would require a new union election whenever more than half of a workforce turns over, count every non-voting employee as a 'no' vote in union elections, require a secret-ballot majority of all employees before any strike, and bar unions from spending dues on politics without written annual consent from each member. Supporters called it a worker-rights bill because it adds secret ballots and opt-out rights; unions and their allies called it a union-elimination bill because of how much harder it would make organizing and bargaining.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who do not want union representation would gain: decertification becomes easier, nonmembers can refuse to subsidize union political activity, and unions must publish audited finances. Employers facing union campaigns would benefit from slower elections, extra hearings, and rules that count abstentions as 'no' votes, making successful organizing rare.

how_it_helps.text: Every represented employee, union member or not, would get a secret-ballot vote on ratifying a contract or going on strike, with the union paying for strike-vote elections.
Union dues could not be spent on anything not directly related to collective bargaining unless a member signs a written authorization, which expires after one year with no automatic renewal.

Unions would face new penalties, including lost wages and liquidated damages, for coercing workers over organizing or decertification, and using force or violence to obtain representation rights would carry fines up to $100,000 and up to 10 years in prison.
Labor unions would have to file independently verified annual audit reports and share records with members and nonmembers alike.

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions would bear most of the cost: fewer successful organizing elections, forced recertification elections after workforce turnover, near-impossible strike thresholds, defunded political activity, and new audit expenses. Workers who rely on union bargaining power would bear the indirect cost if their union weakened or lost certification, and any current contract would terminate if a recertification vote went against the union.

drawbacks.text: The bill redefines 'majority' in a union election to mean a majority of all employees in the unit, not just those voting, so every worker who stays home is counted against the union — a standard no candidate for office would accept.

Requiring recertification elections whenever a unit's workforce turns over by more than 50%, and letting any current contract terminate if the union loses, would make long-term bargaining agreements unstable and give employers repeated chances to shed representation.
Requiring consent of a majority of all represented employees before any strike, with the union paying for the election, would leave unions with little leverage at the bargaining table.
Restricting dues to collective-bargaining purposes only would cut off union political advocacy on minimum wage, safety, and labor-law issues that affect all workers, not just fee-payers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consent and transparency pieces — annual opt-in for political spending, secret ballots on strikes and contracts, audited union finances — respond to a real complaint from workers who are required to pay fees as a condition of employment. But the bill's structural provisions cut far deeper: counting abstentions as 'no' votes, perpetual recertification elections, and near-unanimous strike requirements would have made union organizing and survival extremely difficult while leaving employer power untouched. On balance, the bill was designed to shrink union representation far more than to expand worker choice, and workers who depend on collective bargaining would likely have come out worse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the Employee Rights Act on September 7, 2017, joined by 14 other Republican senators as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
That referral was the bill's last action: the committee never held a hearing or markup, and no vote was ever held in either chamber.
The bill received 31 cosponsors, all Republicans, but died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers who depend on them are better off, because the existing rules that let unions organize, bargain, and spend dues on advocacy remain in force. Employers who would have benefited from weaker unions gained nothing from the bill's death, though they also gave nothing up.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Employee Rights Act and organized 14 fellow Republicans as original cosponsors.

for.name: Coalition for Employee Rights
for.role: Business-backed coalition promoting the bill nationally
for.what_they_did: Promoted the Employee Rights Act as a model worker-rights bill in multiple Congresses and lobbied for its passage.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Took no action after receiving the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 supporters — the sponsor and 31 cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist to measure the floor split.

industries.note: The bill targets nearly every lever of union power: organizing elections, contract longevity, strike authority, dues-funded advocacy, and financial privacy. Unions' interest in stopping it ran alongside the interest of workers who rely on collective bargaining.

industries.industry: Unionized employers and anti-union business coalitions
industries.note: Weaker unions mean fewer successful organizing drives, less bargaining pressure, and more management control over wages and conditions. The gains for employers come directly out of workers' bargaining power.
